A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The only result is the starting architecture, which scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it gives no signal yet. Two problems are likely. First, the default recipe allows only about 32 PPO updates of 4,096 steps each, which is very little feedback for exact multi-brick builds. Second, a good placement depends on the landing layer, which is the highest build cell under the footprint. The brick is good only if the target has exactly those footprint cells at that layer and nothing below gets sealed. The starting head pools features that don't track layers, so it struggles to check this. Round 1 tests the two fixes as a factorial: a head with per-layer footprint pooling under the default recipe, the original network under a recipe with more samples and more frequent updates, and both together. Any result above zero is informative.

### Round 2
All four trials so far score exactly 0, including the training-success figure, so round 1 says nothing about which change helps. The likely cause is that the agent learns too little in very few samples. r1c1's heavier head (r=1.67) also cut its training steps. On paper the task can be solved with local rules. A brick is safe when, at its landing layer L (the highest build height under its footprint), every footprint cell is a target cell, and the target is empty in any gaps between each column's current height and L. Every column-layer pair can then use the same weights if each cell is described relative to L (the column stack shifted so L sits at the centre). This should learn much faster than weights specific to each layer. To keep r≤1 and get the most samples, the network is cheap. I test two recipes. A 3×3 learned head checks whether the brick-anchor convention (or the world itself) differs from the description.

### Round 3
All six trials scored 0 on dev, and training success was also 0. Three different heads (the generic baseline, per-layer pooling, and relative-layer column features) and a learned 3x3 head all failed in the same way. Geometry or architecture therefore does not look like the main limit. One confound runs through every trial: my "data-rich" recipes cut the number of gradient steps, which I did not intend. The default takes about 4.1k Adam steps (32 updates × 4 epochs × 32 minibatches). r1c2 took about 1.9k and r2c2 about 1.7k. With 257 actions and an exact-build goal, the agent probably needs many more policy updates before it gets any successes to learn from. This round tests a recipe with many small minibatches: 64 envs, 16 minibatches of 64 samples, 4 epochs. That is about 8k gradient steps over about 128 updates. I apply it to the baseline net, to the relative-layer net, and to a new, deeper residual trunk that mixes in global context.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored 0 on dev and 0 in training, including the starting network. They covered many recipes and three head designs. The usual explanation, seed noise, cannot cover this, so a structural mismatch is the likely cause. The starting network's 1x1 stem works for any channel order. Its 3x3 trunk can learn small anchor offsets, and r2c3's per-type learned head can learn any type order. What every trial assumed is that the logit vector is laid out as type, then y, then x, lined up with the observation grid. If the world reads actions transposed, flipped or cell-major, a convolutional head cannot learn the mapping. Last round, I test this with a learned gate over common action layouts (flips, transpose, cell-major), with a fully connected head that can learn any layout, and with a hybrid of the two.
